level-1.title: What a mutual fund actually is
summary: A mutual fund pools money from many people. A manager buys shares in many companies with it.
You own a small slice of the whole pool, so one company doing badly does not sink you.
A SIP puts a fixed amount in every month - ₹500, say - instead of one lump sum.
A bank deposit or PPF promises you a number. A mutual fund promises nothing at all.
That is the whole difference. Higher possible growth is paid for with the chance of going down.
Money you need soon should not go in a fund. Money you will not touch for years might.

questions.prompt: A mutual fund invests in 50 different companies. One of those companies goes out of business completely. What is the most likely effect on someone who owns a slice of the whole fund?

image.alt: Many hands putting coins into one pot invested across many companies

options.label: They lose all their money immediately
A small effect - losing one company out of fifty does not sink the whole fund
Nothing changes at all, funds are immune to company failures

questions.hint: Recall why owning a slice of MANY companies protects you, compared to owning just one.

questions.prompt: You need ₹20,000 for a family wedding expense in 4 months. Someone suggests putting it in a mutual fund to 'grow it a bit first.' What is the risk in this specific plan?

image.alt: A calendar with four months marked beside a fund that can rise or fall

options.label: There is no risk, since 4 months is plenty of time for any fund
The only risk is missing out on extra growth
The fund's value could be lower than ₹20,000 exactly when you need it for the wedding

questions.hint: Ask what happens if the fund's value happens to be down on the exact day you need the money.

questions.prompt: Fund A grew 25% last year. Fund B grew only 5% last year. A friend says Fund A is definitely the better choice going forward. What does the lesson say about this reasoning?

image.alt: Two funds with very different growth last year

options.label: It is flawed - past growth does not decide future growth for either fund
Fund B is guaranteed to fail next year
It is correct - the fund that grew more before will always grow more again

questions.hint: The lesson specifically warns against judging future performance by past results.

level-2.title: Risk, time and a fund in your own name
summary: Every place for money trades three things: how much it might grow, how likely you are to lose some, and how fast you can get it back.
A savings account is instant and safe at about 4%. PPF is locked for years at about 7%. A fund could beat both, or lose money - nothing is promised.
Since prices rise around 6% a year, money sitting at 4% is quietly shrinking in what it can buy. Safety is not free either.
A SIP of ₹500 a month is ₹6,000 a year. Its value is whatever the units are worth on the day you sell, which may be more or less than you paid.
A minor can hold a fund. The child is the sole owner and an adult only operates it - no joint holding is allowed.
Two things worth knowing: the folio PAUSES on your eighteenth birthday until you convert it yourself, and money taken out is paid only into a bank account in your own name.
So the account comes first, the emergency savings come second, and the fund comes third. In that order, never reversed.

questions.prompt: PPF pays about 7% but locks your money for years. A savings account pays about 4% but you can withdraw any day. For money you might need within 6 months, which is more suitable, and why?

image.alt: A locked scheme beside an instantly accessible account

options.label: PPF - the higher rate always wins regardless of when you need the money
Both are equally suitable
The savings account - instant access matters more than a higher rate you cannot legally reach in time

questions.hint: A better rate is worthless if the money is locked away exactly when you need it.

questions.prompt: You are 17, hold a SIP in your own name with your mother operating it, and plan to withdraw the money the week after your 18th birthday. What TWO facts affect whether this plan works smoothly?

image.alt: A calendar with an eighteenth birthday circled beside a SIP folio

options.label: Only your mother's signature is needed, nothing else changes at 18
Turning 18 has no effect on a SIP at all
The folio freezes at 18 until converted by you, AND the money can only be paid into an account in your own name

questions.hint: Two separate rules both apply exactly at the moment you turn 18.

questions.prompt: A 16-year-old with ₹5000 and no bank account yet wants to put all of it straight into a mutual fund because 'it grows faster.' What is wrong with this plan?

image.alt: Three numbered steps, with the fund step attempted first

options.label: The plan is fine as long as an adult approves it
A fund cannot even be set up or pay out properly without a bank account in the child's name first
Nothing is wrong, funds should always come first for maximum growth

questions.hint: Recall the exact three-step order given at the end of the lesson, and what has to exist before a fund can work at all.

level-3.title: Spreading risk, and what a fund costs
summary: Diversification means not putting all your money in one place. If one company fails, the others still stand.
A mutual fund already spreads money across many companies. An index fund simply buys every company in a market index.
NAV - net asset value - is the price of one unit of the fund on a given day.
Every fund charges a yearly fee called the expense ratio. A 1% fee sounds small, but it is taken every year, on everything you hold.
Past returns do not promise future returns. A fund that did well last year can fall this year.
Match the risk to the time. Money needed within a year belongs somewhere safe; money for ten years away can take more risk for more growth.
Anyone who promises fixed, high returns from a market-linked fund is not being honest. Market-linked means it can go down.

questions.prompt: Ravi puts all ₹10,000 into one company’s shares. Meena puts ₹10,000 into a fund spread across 50 companies. If one company collapses, who is hurt more?

image.alt: One basket with all the eggs, and many baskets with a few each

options.label: Meena, because her fund is bigger
Ravi, because all his money was in that one company
Both lose exactly the same

questions.hint: What happens when all your eggs are in one basket?

questions.prompt: You will need ₹20,000 for college fees in 8 months. Where should that money be?

image.alt: A calendar with college fees due soon

options.label: Somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a savings account or a short deposit
In a high-risk fund, for the biggest growth
In shares of one company a friend recommends

questions.hint: Can you afford a fall in value just before you need the money?

questions.prompt: An agent says: "This fund is market-linked, but I guarantee 20% a year." What should you think?

options.label: Great - a guarantee means there is no risk
Ask for the guarantee in writing, then invest
Be wary - a market-linked fund cannot promise fixed returns

questions.hint: What does "market-linked" mean for the returns?
